claims.text: In Node.js v24.10.0, server.headersTimeout limits how long the HTTP parser waits to receive the complete request headers. Its default is the minimum of server.requestTimeout and 60,000 ms (60 seconds).
In Node.js v24.10.0, server.requestTimeout is the millisecond limit for receiving the entire request from the client. Its default is 300,000 ms (300 seconds, five minutes).
If either headersTimeout or requestTimeout expires, the server responds with HTTP 408, does not forward the request to the request listener, and closes the connection.

In Node.js v24.10.0, server.timeout measures socket inactivity in milliseconds before the socket is presumed to have timed out. Its default is 0, which disables this timeout behavior on incoming connections. A value change affects new connections, not existing ones.

When a Server 'timeout' listener is present, Node calls it with the timed-out socket; the server documentation says timeouts must then be handled explicitly. The listener is notified of the timeout, so application code is responsible for handling the socket timeout.

No. A 300,000 ms requestTimeout is a deadline for receiving the entire client request, and headersTimeout concerns receiving headers; neither establishes a 300-second deadline for application work after the request reaches its listener. server.timeout is an inactivity timeout on a socket, not a total operation-duration limit. These settings alone therefore do not prove a 300-second application-operation deadline.

note.recommendation: Treat these as distinct transport-level controls: headersTimeout bounds header receipt, requestTimeout bounds complete request receipt, and server.timeout bounds socket inactivity. If an application operation itself needs a 300-second deadline, define and enforce that deadline around the operation separately; the supplied Node.js v24.10.0 documentation does not say these HTTP settings enforce it.
unknowns: The supplied extract does not specify application-level timeout mechanisms or how a particular framework or handler controls work after request parsing.
The source extract is limited to Node.js v24.10.0 HTTP documentation; behavior of other Node.js versions and surrounding proxies or frameworks was not assessed.
